Sanjay — thanks for the brief and attachments. Looping in Naomi & Karthik to pull a short evaluation together.

Initial framing (we'll formalize after a quick call):

1) Decision criteria (attached): throughput/latency, per-byte egress cost, operational complexity (route tables, NAT), security boundary (control vs data), failover behavior, monitoring & traceability, and supportability/SLAs.

2) Quick instincts:
- VPC Peering: good for high-throughput, low-latency egress if both sides are in the same cloud provider and you can accept cross-VPC route table complexity. Limited to inter-VPC routing (no AWS PrivateLink-style service endpoint).
- PrivateLink: strong isolation for control-plane/admin APIs; easiest to audit and limit surface area. Can be more expensive per-GB and requires service endpoint architecture.
- Site-to-Site VPN: useful for on-prem backup lanes or when direct cloud-to-cloud peering isn't possible; adds latency and jitter — acceptable for non-real-time workloads.

3) Consider SD-WAN / managed VPN overlay if customer needs active-active multi-region failover without changing route tables frequently.

Next step: short 30-min call to agree constraints and produce a recommended pattern + diagram + cost delta.

Thanks Marcus — brief notes from my side after quick read of requirements:

Pros/cons (high level):
- Peering:
  * Pros: Lowest latency, straightforward egress for large volumes, fewer middleboxes.
  * Cons: Route table sprawl across VPCs, transitive limitations (can't peer through VPC A to B), lifecycle management when using Dedicated/private deployments across accounts.
- PrivateLink:
  * Pros: Service-level boundary, great for admin/control plane, IAM-friendly, easily audited via endpoint flows.
  * Cons: Higher per-GB cost, needs endpoint services on provider side, additional configuration for multi-AZ redundancy.
- Site-to-Site VPN:
  * Pros: Works for on-prem and when cloud peering prohibited, predictable for batch/backup traffic.
  * Cons: Latency/jitter, throughput caps unless you use appliances or SD-WAN, more opaque for tracing requests back to origin.

SD-WAN thought: if MidwestMed needs active-active failover across on-prem and multiple cloud regions, a managed SD-WAN overlay reduces the need to rework route tables and can provide deterministic failover behavior. See attached cost sketch: swan-cost-scenario.xlsx

I'll join the call and can draft a recommended hybrid: peering for inference traffic (low-latency), PrivateLink for control-plane, and S2S or SD-WAN for on-prem backups.

—Naomi

Short technical note — things to watch for when recommending a hybrid approach:

> From: Naomi Feldman <naomi.feldman@redwood.com>
> Pros/cons (high level):
> - Peering: ...

1) MTU & fragmentation: Peering can surface MTU differences (if customer uses on-prem appliances) — we should verify path MTU and account for L7 proxies that may add headers.
2) Egress billing: ask the cloud provider for inter-VPC egress tiers and include inter-region replication costs. Peering inside same AZ or region is usually cheaper than traversing provider backbone via PrivateLink.
3) Audit & flow logs: PrivateLink endpoints provide cleaner service-level logs; peering requires flow logs across VPCs and aggregation. For HIPAA/regulatory audits, PrivateLink reduces the surface auditors need to inspect.
4) IAM & keying: recommend separating KMS keys for inference logs and control-plane metadata. PrivateLink can enforce IAM on the endpoint; peering cannot.
5) HA patterns: for the inference path we recommend active-active across two AZs with route health checks (BGP or managed route53 health checks) and a small warm standby. For customer failover <90s, SD-WAN or managed BGP session will give the cleanest switchover.

Reference: internal runbook NET-314 (https://redwood.atlassian.net/l/c/NET-314) — contains playbooks for endpoint failover and a sample Terraform module.
